## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Mittāmittajātaka* (Ja 473) is a canonical Jātaka tale belonging to the *Dvādasakanipāta* of the Jātaka collection [Fausböll 1887; Morris 1882]. According to the narrative framework recorded in the commentary, the Buddha delivered the story while dwelling at Jetavana regarding an upright courtier of the king of Kosala who had been falsely slandered by envious rivals [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1887]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta, acting as a wise counselor to King Brahmadatta, resolves the king's doubts by expounding thirty-two signs—the sixteen characteristics of an enemy or foe and the sixteen characteristics of a true friend [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1887]. In the identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), the ancient king is identified as Ānanda and the wise minister as the Bodhisatta [Fausböll 1887].
Maurice Winternitz highlights this Jātaka as an example of gnomic and practical wisdom within the collection, noting that the criteria presented for recognizing a true friend are not distinctly Buddhist in outlook, but rather reflect broader ancient Indian life ideals [Winternitz 1933].
SuttaCentral identifies the earlier *Mittāmittajātaka* (Ja 197) as a passage-level parallel to this text [SuttaCentral]. In DharmaNexus automated text-reuse analysis, the canonical text exhibits extensive Pali reuse with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Vol. 4), sharing 18 passages totaling over 4,600 characters [DharmaNexus]. In cross-language automated alignments, DharmaNexus detects minor shared verse segments with the Sanskrit *Patna Dharmapada* (5 matches) and Śāntideva's *Bodhicaryāvatāra* (7 matches) [DharmaNexus].
